final_proof:
Proof. Write a variable point of the plane as $(X,Y)$. A nonvertical line through the origin whose angle of inclination is $\alpha$ has equation $Y=X\tan\alpha$, while the vertical line has equation $X=0$. (As usual, the inclination of a line is taken modulo $\pi$, with $\pi/2$ representing the vertical line.) Likewise, the line through $P=(x,y)$ parallel to a nonvertical line of inclination $\alpha$ has equation $Y-y=(X-x)\tan\alpha$; if that parallel line is vertical, its equation is $X=x$. Since $M$ and $N$ are distinct lines through the origin, they are not parallel. Consequently, $M$ and the line through $P$ parallel to $N$ have exactly one intersection, so the point calculated below is indeed $\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)$.

First suppose $\theta=\pi/2$. Then $M$ is the vertical line $X=0$. Because $M\ne N$, the line $N$ is nonvertical, and the line through $P$ parallel to $N$ is
\[Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi.\]
At its intersection with $M$ we have $X=0$, and hence $Y=y-x\tan\phi$. Thus
\[\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(0,\,y-x\tan\phi).\]

Next suppose $\phi=\pi/2$. Then $N$ is vertical. Since $M\ne N$, the line $M$ is nonvertical and has equation $Y=X\tan\theta$. The line through $P$ parallel to $N$ is $X=x$, whose intersection with $M$ is therefore
\[\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(x,\,x\tan\theta).\]
(The hypotheses exclude the possibility that both $\theta$ and $\phi$ equal $\pi/2$.)

It remains to consider the case in which neither angle is $\pi/2$. Put
\[Q=\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(u,v).\]
Both lines are then nonvertical. The condition $Q\in M$ and the condition that $Q-P$ be parallel to $N$ give, respectively,
\[v=u\tan\theta,\qquad v-y=(u-x)\tan\phi.\]
Substituting the first equality into the second yields
\[u(\tan\theta-\tan\phi)=y-x\tan\phi.\]
Here $\tan\theta\ne\tan\phi$: otherwise the two nonvertical lines through the origin would have the same slope and hence would be the same line, contrary to $M\ne N$. We may therefore divide to obtain
\[u=\frac{y-x\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}=\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}-\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}.\]
Using $v=u\tan\theta$ gives
\[v=\frac{y\tan\theta-x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}=\frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}-\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}.\]
These are exactly the two coordinates asserted in the third case. Together with the two vertical cases, this proves the stated piecewise formula for every $P\in\mathbb R^2$. $\square$
